I joined Jen Psaki on MS NOW to discuss the hurdles of affordability in North Carolina and the consequences of a recent Supreme Court decision on my race.
Here's how it went.
**Jen Psaki:**_Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in North Carolina, former Governor Roy Cooper. And I want to talk about your race because you are clearly doing something very right, there in North Carolina and the people there have known you a long time. But I just have to ask you, I 've been watching your race. You've been talking about affordability, what people are going through. How does the President of the United States making more than $2 billion while in office resonate with the people of North Carolina?_
**Roy Cooper:**_I think the Washington DC swamp is deeper than ever. Jen, elected leaders should serve the people, not line their pockets, and all of this is occurring at a time when people 's paychecks just simply are not keeping up with the cost of living. No wonder people don't trust the federal government. No wonder people don't trust the administration. They want leaders who are there to serve them. That's what I can do for the people of North Carolina. They've known me for years._
_My opponent, Michael Whatley, who was the RNC chair, and other Republican leaders are letting all of this happen, and many of them are participating in it themselves. Michael Whatley was a longtime DC lobbyist. He lobbied for utility and Big Oil companies. He owns all of the stock. He encouraged the war when gas prices went up. He makes money. He encouraged higher rates for utility companies. When people 's rates go up, he makes money. That's the kind of thing we shouldn't have._
_I am for a Congressional and Executive stock [trading] ban. Regardless of whether a law passes, I 'm not going to own individual stocks. I now have all of mine in widely held mutual funds... We need more people in Washington like this. This is going to be a tough race, so I need people to go to [roycooper.com](https://substack.com/redirect/925c4080-11f2-49f6-b4b5-a3870f07b50d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and help us out._
* * *
If you've read enough, you can watch my full interview here:
[](https://substack.com/redirect/dc9f5e8b-262e-4334-96e1-2a2aa3c42908?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
* * *
**Jen Psaki:**_Yeah. Let me ask you about the race because I 'm sure it's to your frustration. It probably feels good to be up in the polls, but you got to keep people focused on the race. There was actually, the Supreme Court yesterday, they had a number of rulings, but one of their rulings, they struck down restrictions on certain spending limits for political parties and candidates. And we've been working to make sense of all this for people watching too._
_But the New York Times used your particular race as an example of how these new rules would offset the cash advantage your campaign currently has over your opponent you were just talking about, former RNC chairman Michael Whatley, because the RNC can spend unlimited money now and give it to campaigns. What do you want people to understand about how the Supreme Court ruling just changed the game - not just in your race, but in perhaps other races across the country?_
**Roy Cooper:** _This is the worst campaign finance ruling since Citizens United. It essentially allows unlimited money from parties. And that just means the billionaires and those in power are going to have more control over these elections. And that 's why we need people to step up more than ever. Look, I've been in a lot of tough elections in my time as Attorney General and Governor, but this is the toughest one that I've ever been in. In North Carolina in almost 40 years, we've only elected two Democrats to the US Senate. Both of them were one-termers. The last Democrat we elected was in 2008. And as you well remember, Barack Obama won North Carolina that year._
_Already, these outside groups have put in about a $100 million against me and we 've run great candidates for the Senate in the past, but the pattern has been that the Democrats have been ahead, ahead, ahead until they weren't and Republicans often close at the end. People know me; they don't know my opponent that well. This race will tighten just like all of these other swing seats. But if we don't flip North Carolina, we cannot flip the United States Senate. And from all that you've been talking about tonight, it is pretty clear that we need to take back this Legislative Branch, reassert the constitutional authority that the Legislative Branch has. And you do that by taking back the United States Senate._
_So, we need everybody out there working in these swing Senate seats to try and win this. And people can go to[ roycooper.com](https://substack.com/redirect/925c4080-11f2-49f6-b4b5-a3870f07b50d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), see my platform to Make Stuff Cost Less, volunteer for the campaign and also help us financially._
**Jen Psaki:**_Boy, among many things, somebody who supports a stock ban, including one for the President, sounds pretty good on a day like this. Governor Cooper, thank you as always for being here. I really appreciate it._
* * *
As I told Jen, the DC swamp runs deep. Leaders should serve the people, not profit off of them, especially when paychecks for working folks are not keeping up with the cost of living. I called for a stock ban for Congress and the Executive branch and warned that the Supreme Court's new campaign finance ruling will make this the toughest race of my career.
We need independent leaders in Washington. If you're ready to join me in this fight, I hope you'll consider [chipping in](https://substack.com/redirect/40266aa6-56d1-46c8-968d-65d510548307?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) a few dollars or [signing up](https://substack.com/redirect/111eb01e-2b4d-48c3-a336-0e24891fedf1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to knock doors.

Here's how it went. Jen Psaki:Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in North Carolina, former Governor Roy Cooper. And I want to talk about your race because you are clearly doing something very right, there in North Carolina and the people there have known you a long time. But I just have to ask you, I 've been watching your race. You've been talking about affordability, what people are going through. How does the President of the United States making more than $2 billion while in office resonate with the people of North Carolina? Roy Cooper:I think the Washington DC swamp is deeper than ever. Jen, elected leaders should serve the people, not line their pockets, and all of this is occurring at a time when people 's paychecks just simply are not keeping up with the cost of living. No wonder people don't trust the federal government. No wonder people don't trust the administration. They want leaders who are there to serve them. That's what I can do for the people of North Carolina. They've known me for years. My opponent, Michael Whatley, who was the RNC chair, and other Republican leaders are letting all of this happen, and many of them are participating in it themselves. Michael Whatley was a longtime DC lobbyist. He lobbied for utility and Big Oil companies. He owns all of the stock. He encouraged the war when gas prices went up. He makes money. He encouraged higher rates for utility companies. When people 's rates go up, he makes money. That's the kind of thing we shouldn't have. I am for a Congressional and Executive stock [trading] ban. Regardless of whether a law passes, I 'm not going to own individual stocks. I now have all of mine in widely held mutual funds... We need more people in Washington like this. This is going to be a tough race, so I need people to go to and help us out. If you've read enough, you can watch my full interview here: Jen Psaki:Yeah. Let me ask you about the race because I 'm sure it's to your frustration. It probably feels good to be up in the polls, but you got to keep people focused on the race. There was actually, the Supreme Court yesterday, they had a number of rulings, but one of their rulings, they struck down restrictions on certain spending limits for political parties and candidates. And we've been working to make sense of all this for people watching too. But the New York Times used your particular race as an example of how these new rules would offset the cash advantage your campaign currently has over your opponent you were just talking about, former RNC chairman Michael Whatley, because the RNC can spend unlimited money now and give it to campaigns. What do you want people to understand about how the Supreme Court ruling just changed the game - not just in your race, but in perhaps other races across the country? Roy Cooper: This is the worst campaign finance ruling since Citizens United. It essentially allows unlimited money from parties. And that just means the billionaires and those in power are going to have more control over these elections. And that 's why we need people to step up more than ever. Look, I've been in a lot of tough elections in my time as Attorney General and Governor, but this is the toughest one that I've ever been in. In North Carolina in almost 40 years, we've only elected two Democrats to the US Senate. Both of them were one-termers. The last Democrat we elected was in 2008. And as you well remember, Barack Obama won North Carolina that year. Already, these outside groups have put in about a $100 million against me and we 've run great candidates for the Senate in the past, but the pattern has been that the Democrats have been ahead, ahead, ahead until they weren't and Republicans often close at the end. People know me; they don't know my opponent that well. This race will tighten just like all of these other swing seats. But if we don't flip North Carolina, we cannot flip the United States Senate. And from all that you've been talking about tonight, it is pretty clear that we need to take back this Legislative Branch, reassert the constitutional authority that the Legislative Branch has. And you do that by taking back the United States Senate. So, we need everybody out there working in these swing Senate seats to try and win this. And people can go to, see my platform to Make Stuff Cost Less, volunteer for the campaign and also help us financially. Jen Psaki:Boy, among many things, somebody who supports a stock ban, including one for the President, sounds pretty good on a day like this. Governor Cooper, thank you as always for being here. I really appreciate it. * As I told Jen, the DC swamp runs deep. We need independent leaders in Washington. If you're ready to join me in this fight, I hope you'll consider a few dollars or to knock doors. | | | | | | | (C) 2026 Roy Cooper PO Box 1190, Raleigh, NC 27602 ? ?

body:
[1]Justice Democrats

Peter,

I want you to know this victory belongs to every single one of you.

On Tuesday, Denver voters – of all ages, all races, all religions – sent a
clear message: We will not wait.

We will not wait to bring the fight to Donald Trump and the oligarchy.

We will not wait to demand that Congress abolish ICE and pass Medicare for
All.

We will not wait to end the politics of the past. To get big money out of
our elections. To reject Corporate PACs and AIPAC.

And no, we will not wait to end the genocide in Gaza.

We believe that fundamental change can, and will, happen if we fight for
it. If we organize. If we show no fear in standing up for what’s right.

That is the message Denver has sent to the establishment of both parties.
To Donald Trump. To the entire country.

A year ago, a lot of experienced people told us this was impossible. That
you can’t win without corporate PAC money. That you can’t beat a 30-year
incumbent. That the establishment and the oligarchy is just too big and
too powerful to overcome.

But one year, 6,500 volunteers, 100,000 doors, and 500,000 calls later,
you are proof that the power of organized people is greater than the power
of organized money.

I want to thank you all for supporting this campaign and this movement. To
Justice Democrats, Denver DSA, the Working Families Party, to Sunrise, to
our incredible organizing team, the greatest a girl could ever ask for,
that has made history: Thank you for everything you have done to make this
win possible.

I also want to acknowledge Congresswoman Diana DeGette. I am grateful for
her service to Denver and her fight for reproductive freedom. She helped
build the community that welcomed my family to this district, and I’ll
always be grateful for that.

And I want to thank Senator Bernie Sanders for his support, and every
single progressive running for office in Colorado and across the country
for inspiration and solidarity.

[ https://go.justicedemocrats.com/go/140221?c0=jd-em-20260702-1.Pobfoa&refcode=em20260702-37983&amounts=10%2C27%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&t=1002&akid=37983%2E1203867%2EuHAGNC ]Before I say more, will you pitch in a grassroots contribution to
Justice Democrats right now to help them achieve three more primary wins
against the establishment this summer?

I want to tell you something about why this campaign started. Because it
matters for what comes next.

When I wrote a letter defending students’ rights to protest the genocide
in Gaza, my law firm told me: take it down or you’re fired. I didn’t
flinch. Because I stood by every word. And I always will.

I know that will not be the only moment where those in power will tell me
to change my tune, to not rock the boat. That seems to happen a lot in
Congress. But here in Denver we stand by our values, we stand with our
community.

In two days, this country turns 250 years old. I've been thinking a lot
about what that means. Not the fireworks – the promise that this country
belongs to everyone who loves what it stands for. Not just the people born
here. Not just the people who look a certain way. Everyone who believes
that democracy is worth defending and that every person deserves dignity.

I’m about the same age as my dad when he came to this country. Betting on
that promise. He chose Denver as our home because he thought the city
would welcome us. And that same city just voted to send a 29-year-old
recovering lawyer, barista, immigrant, and democratic socialist to
Congress.

The future is being written right now. Nothing is set in stone. Denver won
this week, but this is about something so much bigger than one moment.
This is a movement, and we are just getting started.

[ https://go.justicedemocrats.com/go/140221?c0=jd-em-20260702-1.Pobfoa&refcode=em20260702-37983&amounts=10%2C27%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&amount=5&t=1003&akid=37983%2E1203867%2EuHAGNC ]Now, we have the chance to help three more progressive primary
candidates — Donavan McKinney, Cori Bush, and Justin J. Pearson — win
their primaries next month and fight alongside me in Congress. Let's grow
our ranks even more: donate $5 or whatever you can to elect
more Justice Democrats!

[ https://go.justicedemocrats.com/go/140221?c0=jd-em-20260702-1.Pobfoa&refcode=em20260702-37983&amounts=10%2C27%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&amount=5&t=1022&akid=37983%2E1203867%2EuHAGNC ]Contribute $5

Thank you, all. I am honored to be your voice in DC. Let’s go to work!

In solidarity,

Melat Kiros

[ ]Before I say more, will you pitch in a grassroots contribution to Justice Democrats right now to help them achieve three more primary wins against the establishment this summer? I want to tell you something about why this campaign started. Because it matters for what comes next. When I wrote a letter defending students’ rights to protest the genocide in Gaza, my law firm told me: take it down or you’re fired. I didn’t flinch. Because I stood by every word. And I always will. I know that will not be the only moment where those in power will tell me to change my tune, to not rock the boat. That seems to happen a lot in Congress. But here in Denver we stand by our values, we stand with our community. In two days, this country turns 250 years old. I've been thinking a lot about what that means. Not the fireworks – the promise that this country belongs to everyone who loves what it stands for. Not just the people born here. Not just the people who look a certain way. Everyone who believes that democracy is worth defending and that every person deserves dignity. I’m about the same age as my dad when he came to this country. Betting on that promise. He chose Denver as our home because he thought the city would welcome us. And that same city just voted to send a 29-year-old recovering lawyer, barista, immigrant, and democratic socialist to Congress. The future is being written right now. Nothing is set in stone. Denver won this week, but this is about something so much bigger than one moment. This is a movement, and we are just getting started. [ ]Now, we have the chance to help three more progressive primary candidates — Donavan McKinney, Cori Bush, and Justin J. Pearson — win their primaries next month and fight alongside me in Congress. Let's grow our ranks even more: donate $5 or whatever you can to elect more Justice Democrats! [ ]Contribute $5 Thank you, all. I am honored to be your voice in DC. Let’s go to work! In solidarity, Melat Kiros [ ]Photo of Melat Kiros Contribute to Justice Democrats:

subject: The World Cup shows us how our country's greatest strength is our diversity.

body:
Embracing our nation’s diversity.
#
Peter,
**Right now,_millions_ of Americans are tuned into the World Cup, cheering on the U.S. Men’s National Team — _especially_ after their win last night against Bosnia and Herzegovina!**
Here’s a fun fact: **six of Team USA’s players are foreign-born, and more than half the roster holds dual citizenship. Team USA beautifully reflects the absolute best quality of our country._Our diversity._**
The immigrant and diasporic roots of this team represent what makes America a powerhouse. Yet, under a cruel policy pushed by Donald Trump, the very fabric of our multicultural identity was almost put at risk. Trump tried to strip automatic birthright citizenship from children born in the U.S. to non-citizens. A benefit that more than half of the nation’s team benefits from.
Thankfully, the Supreme Court recently delivered a landmark 6-3 victory for our communities by striking down Trump’s unconstitutional executive order and firmly upholding birthright citizenship.
The highest court in the land reaffirmed what we have always known. This country is deeply rooted in the immigrant experience. Our cultural diversity, our different backgrounds, and our shared values are exactly what make our country great.
This is a historic win worth celebrating, but we can’t afford to get complacent. The anti-immigrant forces behind this administration aren’t going anywhere for a while, and Trump's allies are already looking for backdoor ways to target our communities and suppress voters ahead of the midterms.

Before I ask you to **[make a contribution to our grassroots General Election Fund,](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/134508774/631343385/840821575?refcode=ea.9265ae59-3576-f111-ac9c-000d3a14b6d6&ms=ea.9265ae59-3576-f111-ac9c-000d3a14b6d6&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMTAvMS84MTM2MiIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI5MjY1YWU1OS0zNTc2LWYxMTEtYWM5Yy0wMDBkM2ExNGI2ZDYiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=t0aiVFh-QdFAZVvRu1hiZIDIH2gSclLb7_6SIQNgmKQ=)** I want to reintroduce myself and explain why I hope to earn your support. I came to Colorado over 30 years ago for a job interview, and that decision changed my life forever. It was here that my wife, Heidi, and I raised our two wonderful kids — three, if you count our mostly-well-behaved dog, Zeke. I’ve dedicated my life to public service. And, as the son and grandson of Holocaust survivors, I’m committed to our shared American values of liberty, justice, and the idea that all people should live free from discrimination, hatred, and oppression. My first job after law school was here in Colorado, and it launched my career that included clerking for Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsberg, working for President Obama, and serving as the Dean of the University of Colorado Law School. From that first job to now, I have always believed that Colorado is the best place to live and the ideal place to raise a family. I love our state. And when you love something, you fight for it. **My commitment to fight for Colorado is why I don’t get it when others try to appease and give in to bullies like the President and his cabinet. It does not work, and it’s not what leaders do. Not now, not ever. We must take a stand, not be afraid, and not back down.** I know fighting for what’s right isn’t easy. Fights worth having rarely are. As the People’s Lawyer, I’ve had a lot of practice in these fights. It’s been my job to enforce the rule of law, and no one is above it: not deceitful corporations, not abusive employers, and definitely not the federal government. In fact, as part of upholding the rule of law, I’ve taken the Trump administration to court 67 times (and counting) — and we’re winning again and again. **I’m proud of the reputation I’ve built here in Colorado.** I’m not here to do “politics as usual.” I’m here to fight for you, not the powerful or wealthy few. name: Heidi Ganahl
subject: The Mountain Minute: 7/2/2026
body:
Colorado’s dirty voter roll: Getting on is the easy part
| | | | [](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)
---
**PRESENTED BY[ROCKYMOUNTAINVOICE.COM](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**
| | Hey folks,
Want your full news breakdown? Listen to the Mountain Minute podcast [here](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.), or watch on [YouTube](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) or [Rumble](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.).
**🏔️ Here in Colorado...** The GOP governor's primary stayed too close to call, with Marx edging Kirkmeyer 39.9%-39.4% (Bottoms at 20%); the winner [faces Democrat AG Phil Weiser](), who beat Sen. Bennet, in November. [The bigger shock](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.): 29-year-old democratic socialist Melat Kiros [ousted 15-term Rep. Diana DeGette](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) in Denver's 1st District. Separately, the Tenth Circuit [unanimously rejected the DOJ's no-bond-hearing detention theory](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.), a ruling affecting hundreds of pending Colorado immigration cases and deepening a circuit split headed toward the Supreme Court.
**🇺🇸 On the National Stage...** Tina Peters, freshly released from prison, [met Trump at the White House](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.), where he credited himself with her release and echoed her election-fraud claims. The Supreme Court issued two major rulings: in Watson v. RNC, justices [upheld counting mail ballots postmarked by Election Day but received later](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.); and in a Roberts-authored opinion, the Court [blocked Trump's bid to restrict birthright citizenship](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.), ruling children born here to unlawfully present parents are citizens under the 14th Amendment (Kavanaugh partially dissented).
**🗣️ Commentary Spotlight...** Mike O'Donnell [challenges Colorado's "gold standard" election-integrity reputation](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.), citing rapid voter-roll growth, default automatic registration, and a homeless self-ID loophole allowing unverified addresses. Cory Gaines warns that [2030 census planning leans on the same nonprofit-grant outreach model as 2020](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.), with groups pushing for a bigger role that could skew "hard-to-count" efforts toward Front Range-favored communities.
This is your Mountain Minute for Thursday, July 2, 2026.
– Team RMV
---
|
---
**TODAY'S TOP STORIES**
**[Colorado’s dirty voter roll: Getting on is the easy part](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY MIKE O'DONNELL, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)
[](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)
I’ve spent the last few months digging deeply into the Colorado voter roll from all sorts of different angles and although politicians of a certain party and their supporters are quick to parrot that Colorado exemplifies the “gold standard” of election integrity, that very definitely does NOT appear to be the case after a close examination of Colorado’s voter roll, the rightful starting point for any such assessment of the quality of election integrity in this or any other state.
A closing line from the Eagles’ 1976 hit song ‘Hotel California’ seems to be the most appropriate way to summarize the apparent philosophy behind the approach taken by Colorado’s legislature and the current Secretary of State when it comes to the voter roll: “You can check out any time you like, but you can never leave.”
**[READ MORE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**
|
---
**[Tenth Circuit strikes down DOJ detention theory, ruling affects Colorado courts](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY SHAINA COLE, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)
* The Tenth Circuit ruled that the DOJ's attempt to detain illegal immigrants arrested in the interior without bond hearings exceeded its statutory authority, rejecting a reading of immigration law that every presidential administration for nearly 30 years had declined to adopt — and that Congress itself didn't expand when it passed the Laken Riley Act in January 2025.
* The ruling directly impacts 722 pending petitions in Colorado alone, where district judges had already rejected the government's theory in 248 of 248 resolved cases — and now those wins carry full appellate authority, with the Supreme Court likely the only venue that can settle the deepening circuit split.
* In a costly consequence for taxpayers, every attorney who secured one of those 248 wins is now eligible to seek legal fees from the federal government under the Equal Access to Justice Act — with total fee exposure still uncalculated but the legal basis for collecting confirmed by the Tenth Circuit.

Will you split a donation between Equal Opportunity Now and my campaign for U.S. Senate in Alaska? No matter how much you can afford to chip in today, it all adds up when lots of us are chipping in. [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/eon-peltola]

Thanks for being a part of it.
- Mary

| Peter,

Let’s say the quiet part out loud: **The US Supreme Court is broken.**

Over the last several years, we've watched a handful of unelected justices chip away at fundamental rights, bend over backwards for Donald Trump, and become mired in ethics scandals that would get almost anyone else fired.

_That's not justice. That's a crisis of accountability._

**I'm running for Congress because I believe no one in America should be above the law – not even the people whose job is to interpret it.

[_If you're ready to shake up Washington and restore accountability, will you chip in $10 or whatever you can today?_](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/134510934/631350775/680287355?refcode=BLU_EM_MOSS_2026-07-02_1&amount=10&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNjIvMS8xMTc5OTIiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiN2MzNGY0NDYtMzg3Ni1mMTExLWFjOWMtMDAwZDNhMTRiNmQ2IiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=7Vv-YuvYrV4dMBpu7hCpfXsqPNSAD_HjrMGsLdtuHT0=)**

Here's where I stand. No one should hold that much power for life.

And I support real, enforceable ethics rules, a binding code of conduct, and full financial transparency for every justice on the Court – the same standards that already apply to every other federal judge.

_This shouldn't be controversial._

Public trust in our institutions depends on accountability. If the Supreme Court expects Americans to follow the law, the least its members can do is follow basic ethical standards themselves.

For too long, politicians in Washington have treated the Court like it's untouchable. I don't.

clean_body: | = | Peter, Let’s say the quiet part out loud: The US Supreme Court is broken. Over the last several years, we've watched a handful of unelected justices chip away at fundamental rights, bend over backwards for Donald Trump, and become mired in ethics scandals that would get almost anyone else fired. That's not justice. That's a crisis of accountability. I'm running for Congress because I believe no one in America should be above the law – not even the people whose job is to interpret it. = | = Here's where I stand. = I support a mandatory retirement age for Supreme Court justices, just like we have for judges here in Michigan. No one should hold that much power for life. And I support real, enforceable ethics rules, a binding code of conduct, and full financial transparency for every justice on the Court – the same standards that already apply to every other federal judge. This shouldn't be controversial. Public trust in our institutions depends on accountability. If the Supreme Court expects Americans to follow the law, the least its members can do is follow basic ethical standards themselves. For too long, politicians in Washington have treated the Court like it's untouchable. Here is the story we have been told about the American Dream: it was real once, then the world changed, and now things are simply harder. Globalization happened. Technology happened. Prices went up while wages didn't. Housing got unaffordable. Healthcare got complicated. And that is just how things are now -- unfortunate, perhaps, but inevitable. The kind of change that happens to a country the way weather happens, without anyone being particularly responsible for it.
I don't accept that story. Not because I haven't seen the damage -- I've spent twenty years in affordable housing development, addiction treatment, farming and food systems, geopolitical research and analysis for the State Department, cooperative economics, and community organizing, and I have seen the damage up close. But I have also watched closely enough to know that systems don't drift on their own. They respond to the forces applied to them. And the forces applied to the American economy, to American government, and to the lives of ordinary Americans over the past four decades were not acts of God.
They were acts of Congress.
Things don't simply _happen_. Corporations pay lobbyists. Congress writes laws. Presidents sign them. Agencies enforce them. Courts interpret them. That is policy. And over the course of decades, **policy** changed the trajectory of this country -- not all at once, not through any single dramatic rupture, but through a long accumulation of choices, each one shifting America a little more from workers to shareholders, from communities to corporations, from the public interest to private capture.
Which means **policy can change it back.**
That is the argument I want to make here -- a coherent account of what happened, and what repair looks like. Because I believe this moment requires exactly that: a clear causal story that connects the frustration you feel about **housing** to the frustration you feel about **healthcare** to the frustration you feel about **government** , and shows you that they share a cause - and a solution.
My detailed platform is on my website, [www.VoteMelissa4Congress.com](https://substack.com/redirect/45458e7b-7c33-49b0-a471-f538cafa565e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/5be4050b-62fa-401d-9878-db599060717d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|

* * *
## What Policy Did
Start with money and power, because that is where most of the damage originates.
Over several decades, Congress progressively loosened antitrust enforcement while simultaneously allowing unlimited corporate money into politics. (The Supreme Court has poured fuel on the fire.) Those two decisions compounded each other in ways that can only be untangled by Congress. When industries can consolidate without limit, and then use that consolidated wealth to influence the people writing the rules, the result is what you see today: markets that reward gatekeeping over innovation and creativity, legislative bodies where the donor class's priorities reliably outrank constituents' needs, and an economy where productivity keeps rising while the wages of the people producing it stay flat.
**The housing crisis of 2008, and subsequent global financial crisis, was not a natural disaster**. It was created by Congressional permission for Wall Street to gamble with other people's money. It was the predictable consequence of treating housing as a leveraged financialized instrument rather than a social good -- of allowing institutional investors to outcompete first-time buyers with cash; of zoning codes and expensive, time-consuming permitting regimes that locked in scarcity by design; of decades of disinvestment in the public and nonprofit housing sectors that once sheltered millions of working Americans. When homes become nothing but an gambling vehicle of choice for private equity seeking yield, then ordinary families who need places to live find themselves competing with corporations who don't have a ceiling on their budget.
**The healthcare crisis is the same story told through a different industry.** The United States spends more per person on healthcare than any other developed nation, and gets worse outcomes than most of them. (The cost of our health insurance system _alone_ -- profiteering middlemen who contribute absolutely nothing and put time-consuming, wasteful, and sometimes deadly barriers between people who need care and people who provide it -- is over $1.2 trillion per year.) The gap between what we spend and what we receive is not a mystery. It is the cost of a system designed around parasitic profit extraction rather than genuine health for all people: pharmaceutical monopolies, labyrinthine administrative overhead, fragmented coverage, and the systematic subordination of patient outcomes to shareholder return. Every other major developed democracy has solved this problem. The idea that we cannot is a failure of political will, not a law of nature.
**And then there are the wars.** (Of note: Congress, which possesses the Constitutional authority to declare war, has not done so since 1942.) Since the Authorization for Use of Military Force in 2001, multiple trillions of dollars have flowed to contractors, occupations, and operations that have not made us safer. Every dollar spent on a war that should never have been fought is a dollar not invested in hospitals, schools, roads, veterans' care, and the communities that sent their children to fight, suffer disabling injuries, or die. As the daughter of a retired Navy Commander and the wife of an honorable, 100% disabled American Military veteran in wheelchair -- a man who served his country faithfully and was then illegally abducted by ICE and held for 124 days, until a federal judge ordered his immediate release, calling the detention "flat out wrong" -- I can tell you with fire and precision the human cost of America's decision to spend its political will projecting power abroad instead of caring for people at home.
None of this was inevitable. Each crisis had authors. Each policy had Congressional sponsors. Each law had beneficiaries. And overwhelmingly, they were not you.

* * *
## The Word I Keep Returning To
When I was building out my platform for this race, I kept returning to a single word.
_Repair._
I'm a land steward. I've grown food, tended a young orchard, and cared for the soil using permaculture principles -- working with natural systems rather than against them, building soil health rather than depleting it, designing for resilience rather than extraction. I know what it means to restore depleted land: to do the patient, unglamorous work of returning organic matter and microbial life to ground that has been farmed without care, until it can hold water again, sustain roots again, produce food again. That work requires diligence, long-term thinking, and a strong back. It also requires an honest diagnosis before anything else -- you cannot repair what you will not look at clearly.
**Repair is not nostalgia.** It is not a wish to return to some imagined golden past, as if the original American economy were something we should want to reconstruct wholesale. (It wasn't.) It is something more demanding and more honest than that: the willingness to understand what a system was designed to do, identify where and why it failed, and do the skilled, careful work of restoring its function.
The American Constitution, at its core, is a serious attempt to build a government that could not be captured by any faction, that could not be inherited by any dynasty or aristocracy, that had to continuously _earn_ its legitimacy in the eyes of We the People. The American ideals of **liberty, equality, and justice under law are worth defending** -- which is precisely why their corruption by concentrated money and power is such a profound betrayal of what this country is supposed to be.
You do not abandon a Democratic, Constitutional Republic because it has been corrupted. You **repair** it, because the thing underneath the corruption is worth saving.
That is what this campaign is about. Not revolution: not the wholesale destruction of institutions that, even damaged, represent centuries of hard-won democratic infrastructure. And not the false comfort of incrementalism that asks you to settle for less than you deserve and less than this country is capable of. _**Repair**_ -- serious, evidence-based, people-first repair of the systems that were built to serve you and have been redirected to serve someone else.
Here is what that looks like.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9tZWxpc3NhNGNvbmdyZXNzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.qsdh6mW4M8nxGeWA6fgGS6U-0Z5i7MEepk1l7dlkffg?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=204540233)
* * *
## 01 | Restore the Constitution. Restore Accountability.
The Constitution was not designed to protect the powerful from accountability. It was designed to **protect ordinary people from concentrated power** -- which is why its framers were so deliberate about checks and balances, separation of powers, and the principle that no person or institution stands above the law.
That principle has eroded badly. We have members of Congress trading stocks on privileged knowledge they gathered while writing legislation. We have a Supreme Court operating under ethics rules so weak they are functionally optional. We have presidential administrations that assert authority the Constitution never granted. We have a campaign finance system in which corporations and billionaires can purchase legislative priorities at a scale that makes ordinary constituent voices almost impossible to hear.
Repair means campaign finance reform -- overturning Citizens United, public funding of elections, ending dark money in politics. It means a congressional stock trading ban, with teeth. It means Supreme Court reform with real ethics enforcement, 18-year terms, and mandatory retirement. It means protecting whistleblowers, expanding voting rights, and restoring the full power of Congress to function as the co-equal branch of government it was designed to be.
These are not ideological positions. They are the minimum conditions for a government that is actually accountable to the people it represents. Polling consistently shows that large majorities of Americans, across party lines, support every one of them.
* * *
## 02 | Defend Freedom and Human Dignity.
Freedom is not merely the absence of government interference. It is the positive assurance that your family, your body, your conscience, your home, and your private life belong to you -- not to politicians, not to ideological movements, and not to corporations that harvest your data and monetize your attention without your meaningful consent.
I believe in the First Amendment and the Fourth Amendment with equal conviction. Warrantless surveillance of Americans **needs to end.** Facial recognition in public spaces, predictive policing algorithms, and AI-enabled threat scoring of civilians are incompatible with a free society -- full stop. So is a detention and deportation system that can disappear tens of thousands of people without due process or humane treatment. So is a government that decides one religion's values should govern everyone's medical decisions. Separation of Church and State is not optional.
**Real freedom requires real protection** -- for everyone, regardless of faith, origin, documentation status, or who they love. Immigrants make America stronger; the data on this is unambiguous and has been for generations. Human beings are not a revenue stream, and detention centers run for profit are an American betrayal. Freedom and human dignity are not privileges distributed by political favor. They are rights. It's time Congress started acting accordingly.
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=3260111&post_id=204540233&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjA0NTQwMjMzLCJpYXQiOjE3ODMwMTIzMTgsImV4cCI6MTc4NTYwNDMxOCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTMyNjAxMTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.LM2_FSRk4sHzgWAq9tGUgMXmfuUJk4p-1Uo4yFRGRAg)
* * *
## 03 | Make Life Affordable Again.
The promise at the heart of the American Dream was never luxury. It was _sufficiency_ : the assurance that honest work could sustain a dignified life. One decent job. A home you could afford to keep. Healthcare when you were sick. A school worth attending. A retirement you could actually reach. The ability to raise children without financial terror as a constant background condition of your daily life.
That promise did not fade because Americans stopped working hard enough. Far from it. It was eroded by a long series of Congressional policy choices that made everything essential -- housing, healthcare, childcare, education, retirement, food, energy -- more expensive relative to wages, while systematically shifting risk burden from institutions onto families.
Repairing it means: universal healthcare as a matter of basic social infrastructure; serious investment in housing supply including community land trusts that keep neighborhoods permanently affordable; public options for goods and services in every domain where markets reliably fail people; Right to Repair laws that let you fix the equipment you own; and a Social Security system restored to full solvency that keeps the commitments Americans spent their working lives paying into.
These things are not utopian. They are the standard operating conditions of every other wealthy democracy on earth.
* * *
## 04 | End Wars. Build America.
Every unnecessary war costs us -- in human life, in international standing, in American integrity, in war debt and war taxes (often disguised as inflation), and in the investment here at home that never happened. Roads not built. Schools not funded. Healthcare not provided. Veterans not adequately cared for. Infrastructure left crumbling. Innovation and creativity stalled. Disasters not prepared for. The communities that send the most children to fight consistently receive the least from the budgets those wars consume.
I believe in a strong national _defense_ - not offense. I also believe the Constitution is unambiguous: **Congress declares war**. Never one person, even if they happen to occupy the presidency.
Restoring war powers to Congress is not a retreat from strength -- it is the _requirement_ of a democratic Republic, and a necessary check on the defense contractors who profit from war and violence, and who have spent decades cultivating the Congressional relationships that keep the money flowing... including Congressman "AIPAC Adam" Smith, who I'm running to unseat.
An audit of Pentagon spending, a ban on weapons manufacturer donations to politicians, and a serious commitment to multilateral diplomacy are not soft positions. They are what "America first" actually looks like when it's real -- when you mean it as a budget priority rather than a slogan.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9tZWxpc3NhNGNvbmdyZXNzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.qsdh6mW4M8nxGeWA6fgGS6U-0Z5i7MEepk1l7dlkffg?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=204540233)
* * *
## 05 | Government and Corporations OUT of Your Private Life.
The government has no business in your bedroom, your doctor's office, your religious practice, or your personal convictions. Neither does a corporation. Both the state and the market have expanded into domains they do not belong in, and the Bill of Rights -- properly enforced -- covers both.
Your data is _your property_. The Fourth Amendment protects you from unreasonable search and seizure of your effects, and **no terms of service agreement can waive a constitutional right**. Your body is your domain. Your conscience belongs to you. Government that is prohibited from establishing a state religion is also prohibited from encoding one religion's teachings into law and applying them to everyone.
These are not only progressive positions or conservative positions. They are **constitutional** positions **--** and recovering them requires Members of Congress who do not accept corporate money, and therefore are willing to enforce the Constitution against the interests of the powerful.
* * *
## 06 | Build an Economy That Works for Everyone.
An economy is not an end in itself. It is a system for helping human beings flourish on a living planet, and a system should be judged by whether it actually does its job. An economy that produces record corporate profits alongside record rates of financial anxiety among working families, that has more billionaires (and now trillionaires) than at any point in human history while half of Americans cannot cover a $1,000 emergency without debt -- that economy is failing at its core function, regardless of what the stock market says.
I have spent years working in cooperative economics -- the Mondragon model, community land trusts, employee ownership structures -- and I know from direct experience that the argument that worker ownership is impractical is simply not true. It works.
The economy we _should_ be building creates owners, builders, workers, farmers, inventors, and entrepreneurs, **not simply a class of financial intermediaries extracting rent from every transaction** between producers and consumers.
That requires enforcing antitrust laws with seriousness, supporting cooperatives and ESOPs, investing in apprenticeships in every trade that needs workers, raising the minimum wage to reflect what dignity actually costs, and strengthening the labor movement -- one of the few historical forces that has consistently and effectively counterbalanced concentrated economic power.
[Leave a comment](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=3260111&post_id=204540233&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&isFreemail=true&comments=true&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjA0NTQwMjMzLCJpYXQiOjE3ODMwMTIzMTgsImV4cCI6MTc4NTYwNDMxOCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTMyNjAxMTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.LM2_FSRk4sHzgWAq9tGUgMXmfuUJk4p-1Uo4yFRGRAg&r=1hvr60&utm_campaign=email-half-magic-comments&action=post-comment)
* * *
## 07 | A Thriving Planet Is National Security.
Healthy soil, clean water, a stable climate, and resilient food systems are not luxuries or ideological preferences. **They are the physical substrate on which every other human project depends.** When I practice permaculture, I am not doing something radical -- I am doing something ancient: **taking responsibility for the ground I stand on, so that it can sustain what comes after me.**
That same ethic, applied at national scale, looks like treating climate resilience as critical infrastructure rather than as a political controversy. It looks like transitioning to clean energy not because it is fashionable but because **energy independence and supply-chain resilience are strategic imperatives**. It looks like supporting regenerative agriculture and local food systems, protecting public lands from privatization, fully funding FEMA and disaster preparedness, and leading -- rather than abandoning -- international climate cooperation.
The communities hit hardest by drought, flood, and wildfire are overwhelmingly the communities least able to recover on their own. Climate justice is not a slogan. It is the accurate description of who pays the price when we get this wrong.
* * *
## 08 | Government That Actually Works.
Government exists because there are things free people cannot accomplish alone: issuing currency, defending the country, maintaining the rule of law, building infrastructure, responding to disasters, providing a social safety net, and preventing any private entity from becoming so powerful it can override the public interest. Those are real and legitimate functions. They require a government that is competent, transparent, and genuinely oriented toward solving problems -- rather than protecting insiders, serving donors, or perpetuating its own dysfunction.
The opposite of corrupt government is not "no government." It is GOOD government: agencies that operate honestly and transparently, oversight that genuinely protects the public interest, public services that deliver what they promise, and Representatives who are accountable to constituents rather than to the industries they're supposed to regulate.
We need to end the revolving door between government and the private sector. End gerrymandering. Enact ranked-choice voting, so people can vote for who they really want without fear of "spoilers". Measure what government actually delivers for people, and hold it accountable when it doesn't.
**These are achievable reforms.** They require political will -- and Representatives willing to apply that will in service to the American people, even against their own institutional interests when necessary.
* * *
## Why Repair, and Not Revolution
I want to be precise about why I use the word _repair_ rather than _transform_ or _reimagine_ or any of the other words that get attached to political ambition. It is thoughtfulness. It is honesty. It is a statement of relationship.
**You repair something because you believe it is worth saving.** Because its original design contains something valuable, even if it was imperfect to start with, even if years of neglect or intentional abuse have compromised its function. **The American Constitution, despite its shortcomings, is a serious and sophisticated attempt to build a government that cannot be permanently captured by any faction, that cannot be inherited by dynasties, that must continuously re-earn the consent of the governed.** The American ideals of liberty, equality, and justice under law -- imperfectly realized from the beginning, yes, and requiring ongoing work to extend to everyone they were supposed to include -- _are worth fighting for_. Not as they exist now, but as they were meant to be. As they should be.
America is not disposable. She is not broken beyond repair. But she will not repair herself. And _**the people who profit from her remaining broken**_ -- who benefit from a campaign finance system that makes corruption legal, from monopolies that face no competition, from wars that generate private profit for weapons companies and corrupt politicians, from a healthcare system that bankrupts you for being sick or injured -- _have every incentive to convince you that either nothing is wrong or nothing can be done._ **Both of those claims are false.**
Policy made the system that is failing you. Policy, written by Representatives who are genuinely accountable to you rather than to corporate donors, can repair it.
That is not a utopian promise. It is natural reality. It's an observation about how democratic self-governance is supposed to work.
It is past time we made it work that way again.
* * *
_Melissa Chaudhry is a proven "Lioness for Justice," pro-se litigant and winner, Constitutional Democrat, community-rooted leader, published author, and public servant running for Washington's 9th Congressional District._
_The daughter of a retired US Naval Commander and international humanitarian physician, and the wife of a Melissa 's family story spans the full sweep of American history: her mother's roots trace to the Mayflower; her grandfather survived more than two years of Nazi concentration camp torture before coming to the US without papers. He died of those wounds in America. _
_She 's invested twenty years of her life learning what it actually takes to design economic, political, and societal systems that provide dignity, safety, and opportunity for all people on a living planet. She worked professionally in **affordable housing, climate resilience, sustainable agriculture, ecological design, public health, addiction treatment, poverty alleviation, and immigrant support.** She spent years researching and writing weekly Global Geopolitical Human Security reports distributed to thousands of senior US officials and ambassadors worldwide. She has taught farming, resilient food systems, aquaponics, green infrastructure, and cooperative economics across multiple continents -- and in her own community, she repairs homes, gardens, and vehicles free of charge for friends, elderly and poor. _
_When her honorable, 100% disabled American Military veteran husband, Zahid Chaudhry -- the disabled veteran in wheelchair who has been in America for 30+ years, always come here legally, never broken any US laws EVER, and has had his citizenship [illegally withheld for 25 years](https://substack.com/redirect/6f8e6acd-3400-431b-a18b-dc90f3831bb0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) -- was illegally abducted and detained by ICE in 2025, she singlehandedly fought _Pro Se _across four federal courts and jurisdictions, up against the weaponized federal government, Justice Department, US Attorney General, and ICE**simultaneously** , for four months until a federal judge called his detention "flat out wrong." _
_She and her husband live in South Seattle with their two small children._
_She is the author of_ [Service & Sacrifice: One American Soldier's Fight to Defend the US Constitution](https://substack.com/redirect/27f47d9f-af17-4334-a96e-8f0d3f5ef947?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). _Learn more about her campaign - and sign up to volunteer! - at[ www.VoteMelissa4Congress.com](https://substack.com/redirect/d1bd4d34-e1c9-424a-bb08-d407fbf1ac62?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)._

What policy destroyed, policy can repair. | | | Jul 2 | | | | | | | | | | | | Here is the story we have been told about the American Dream: it was real once, then the world changed, and now things are simply harder. Globalization happened. Technology happened. Prices went up while wages didn't. Housing got unaffordable. Healthcare got complicated. And that is just how things are now -- unfortunate, perhaps, but inevitable. The kind of change that happens to a country the way weather happens, without anyone being particularly responsible for it. I don't accept that story. Not because I haven't seen the damage -- I've spent twenty years in affordable housing development, addiction treatment, farming and food systems, geopolitical research and analysis for the State Department, cooperative economics, and community organizing, and I have seen the damage up close. But I have also watched closely enough to know that systems don't drift on their own. They respond to the forces applied to them. And the forces applied to the American economy, to American government, and to the lives of ordinary Americans over the past four decades were not acts of God. They were acts of Congress. Things don't simply happen. Corporations pay lobbyists. Congress writes laws. Presidents sign them. Agencies enforce them. Courts interpret them. That is policy. And over the course of decades, policy changed the trajectory of this country -- not all at once, not through any single dramatic rupture, but through a long accumulation of choices, each one shifting America a little more from workers to shareholders, from communities to corporations, from the public interest to private capture. Which means policy can change it back. That is the argument I want to make here -- a coherent account of what happened, and what repair looks like. Because I believe this moment requires exactly that: a clear causal story that connects the frustration you feel about housing to the frustration you feel about healthcare to the frustration you feel about government , and shows you that they share a cause - and a solution. My detailed platform is on my website, . | | ---|---|--- What Policy Did Start with money and power, because that is where most of the damage originates. Over several decades, Congress progressively loosened antitrust enforcement while simultaneously allowing unlimited corporate money into politics. (The Supreme Court has poured fuel on the fire.) Those two decisions compounded each other in ways that can only be untangled by Congress. When industries can consolidate without limit, and then use that consolidated wealth to influence the people writing the rules, the result is what you see today: markets that reward gatekeeping over innovation and creativity, legislative bodies where the donor class's priorities reliably outrank constituents' needs, and an economy where productivity keeps rising while the wages of the people producing it stay flat. The housing crisis of 2008, and subsequent global financial crisis, was not a natural disaster. It was created by Congressional permission for Wall Street to gamble with other people's money. It was the predictable consequence of treating housing as a leveraged financialized instrument rather than a social good -- of allowing institutional investors to outcompete first-time buyers with cash; of zoning codes and expensive, time-consuming permitting regimes that locked in scarcity by design; of decades of disinvestment in the public and nonprofit housing sectors that once sheltered millions of working Americans. When homes become nothing but an gambling vehicle of choice for private equity seeking yield, then ordinary families who need places to live find themselves competing with corporations who don't have a ceiling on their budget. The healthcare crisis is the same story told through a different industry. The United States spends more per person on healthcare than any other developed nation, and gets worse outcomes than most of them. (The cost of our health insurance system alone -- profiteering middlemen who contribute absolutely nothing and put time-consuming, wasteful, and sometimes deadly barriers between people who need care and people who provide it -- is over $1.2 trillion per year.) The gap between what we spend and what we receive is not a mystery. It is the cost of a system designed around parasitic profit extraction rather than genuine health for all people: pharmaceutical monopolies, labyrinthine administrative overhead, fragmented coverage, and the systematic subordination of patient outcomes to shareholder return. Every other major developed democracy has solved this problem. The idea that we cannot is a failure of political will, not a law of nature. And then there are the wars. (Of note: Congress, which possesses the Constitutional authority to declare war, has not done so since 1942.) Since the Authorization for Use of Military Force in 2001, multiple trillions of dollars have flowed to contractors, occupations, and operations that have not made us safer. Every dollar spent on a war that should never have been fought is a dollar not invested in hospitals, schools, roads, veterans' care, and the communities that sent their children to fight, suffer disabling injuries, or die. As the daughter of a retired Navy Commander and the wife of an honorable, 100% disabled American Military veteran in wheelchair -- a man who served his country faithfully and was then illegally abducted by ICE and held for 124 days, until a federal judge ordered his immediate release, calling the detention "flat out wrong" -- I can tell you with fire and precision the human cost of America's decision to spend its political will projecting power abroad instead of caring for people at home. None of this was inevitable. Each crisis had authors. Each policy had Congressional sponsors. Each law had beneficiaries. And overwhelmingly, they were not you. The Word I Keep Returning To When I was building out my platform for this race, I kept returning to a single word. Repair. I'm a land steward. I've grown food, tended a young orchard, and cared for the soil using permaculture principles -- working with natural systems rather than against them, building soil health rather than depleting it, designing for resilience rather than extraction. I know what it means to restore depleted land: to do the patient, unglamorous work of returning organic matter and microbial life to ground that has been farmed without care, until it can hold water again, sustain roots again, produce food again. That work requires diligence, long-term thinking, and a strong back. It also requires an honest diagnosis before anything else -- you cannot repair what you will not look at clearly. Repair is not nostalgia. It is not a wish to return to some imagined golden past, as if the original American economy were something we should want to reconstruct wholesale. (It wasn't.) It is something more demanding and more honest than that: the willingness to understand what a system was designed to do, identify where and why it failed, and do the skilled, careful work of restoring its function. The American Constitution, at its core, is a serious attempt to build a government that could not be captured by any faction, that could not be inherited by any dynasty or aristocracy, that had to continuously earn its legitimacy in the eyes of We the People. The American ideals of liberty, equality, and justice under law are worth defending -- which is precisely why their corruption by concentrated money and power is such a profound betrayal of what this country is supposed to be. You do not abandon a Democratic, Constitutional Republic because it has been corrupted. You repair it, because the thing underneath the corruption is worth saving. That is what this campaign is about. Not revolution: not the wholesale destruction of institutions that, even damaged, represent centuries of hard-won democratic infrastructure. And not the false comfort of incrementalism that asks you to settle for less than you deserve and less than this country is capable of. Repair -- serious, evidence-based, people-first repair of the systems that were built to serve you and have been redirected to serve someone else. Here is what that looks like. 01 | Restore the Constitution. Restore Accountability. The Constitution was not designed to protect the powerful from accountability. It was designed to protect ordinary people from concentrated power -- which is why its framers were so deliberate about checks and balances, separation of powers, and the principle that no person or institution stands above the law. That principle has eroded badly. We have members of Congress trading stocks on privileged knowledge they gathered while writing legislation. We have a Supreme Court operating under ethics rules so weak they are functionally optional. We have presidential administrations that assert authority the Constitution never granted. We have a campaign finance system in which corporations and billionaires can purchase legislative priorities at a scale that makes ordinary constituent voices almost impossible to hear. Repair means campaign finance reform -- overturning Citizens United, public funding of elections, ending dark money in politics. It means a congressional stock trading ban, with teeth. It means Supreme Court reform with real ethics enforcement, 18-year terms, and mandatory retirement. It means protecting whistleblowers, expanding voting rights, and restoring the full power of Congress to function as the co-equal branch of government it was designed to be. These are not ideological positions. They are the minimum conditions for a government that is actually accountable to the people it represents. Polling consistently shows that large majorities of Americans, across party lines, support every one of them. 02 | Defend Freedom and Human Dignity. Freedom is not merely the absence of government interference. It is the positive assurance that your family, your body, your conscience, your home, and your private life belong to you -- not to politicians, not to ideological movements, and not to corporations that harvest your data and monetize your attention without your meaningful consent. I believe in the First Amendment and the Fourth Amendment with equal conviction. Warrantless surveillance of Americans needs to end. Facial recognition in public spaces, predictive policing algorithms, and AI-enabled threat scoring of civilians are incompatible with a free society -- full stop. So is a detention and deportation system that can disappear tens of thousands of people without due process or humane treatment. So is a government that decides one religion's values should govern everyone's medical decisions. Separation of Church and State is not optional. Real freedom requires real protection -- for everyone, regardless of faith, origin, documentation status, or who they love. Immigrants make America stronger; the data on this is unambiguous and has been for generations. Human beings are not a revenue stream, and detention centers run for profit are an American betrayal. Freedom and human dignity are not privileges distributed by political favor. They are rights. It's time Congress started acting accordingly. 03 | Make Life Affordable Again. The promise at the heart of the American Dream was never luxury. It was sufficiency : the assurance that honest work could sustain a dignified life. One decent job. A home you could afford to keep. Healthcare when you were sick. A school worth attending. A retirement you could actually reach. The ability to raise children without financial terror as a constant background condition of your daily life. That promise did not fade because Americans stopped working hard enough. Far from it. It was eroded by a long series of Congressional policy choices that made everything essential -- housing, healthcare, childcare, education, retirement, food, energy -- more expensive relative to wages, while systematically shifting risk burden from institutions onto families. Repairing it means: universal healthcare as a matter of basic social infrastructure; serious investment in housing supply including community land trusts that keep neighborhoods permanently affordable; public options for goods and services in every domain where markets reliably fail people; Right to Repair laws that let you fix the equipment you own; and a Social Security system restored to full solvency that keeps the commitments Americans spent their working lives paying into. These things are not utopian. They are the standard operating conditions of every other wealthy democracy on earth. 04 | End Wars. Build America. Every unnecessary war costs us -- in human life, in international standing, in American integrity, in war debt and war taxes (often disguised as inflation), and in the investment here at home that never happened. Roads not built. Schools not funded. Healthcare not provided. Veterans not adequately cared for. Infrastructure left crumbling. Innovation and creativity stalled. Disasters not prepared for. The communities that send the most children to fight consistently receive the least from the budgets those wars consume. I believe in a strong national defense - not offense. I also believe the Constitution is unambiguous: Congress declares war. Never one person, even if they happen to occupy the presidency. Restoring war powers to Congress is not a retreat from strength -- it is the requirement of a democratic Republic, and a necessary check on the defense contractors who profit from war and violence, and who have spent decades cultivating the Congressional relationships that keep the money flowing... including Congressman "AIPAC Adam" Smith, who I'm running to unseat. An audit of Pentagon spending, a ban on weapons manufacturer donations to politicians, and a serious commitment to multilateral diplomacy are not soft positions. They are what "America first" actually looks like when it's real -- when you mean it as a budget priority rather than a slogan. 05 | Government and Corporations OUT of Your Private Life. The government has no business in your bedroom, your doctor's office, your religious practice, or your personal convictions. Neither does a corporation. Both the state and the market have expanded into domains they do not belong in, and the Bill of Rights -- properly enforced -- covers both. Your data is your property. The Fourth Amendment protects you from unreasonable search and seizure of your effects, and no terms of service agreement can waive a constitutional right. Your body is your domain. Your conscience belongs to you. Government that is prohibited from establishing a state religion is also prohibited from encoding one religion's teachings into law and applying them to everyone. These are not only progressive positions or conservative positions. They are constitutional positions -- and recovering them requires Members of Congress who do not accept corporate money, and therefore are willing to enforce the Constitution against the interests of the powerful. 06 | Build an Economy That Works for Everyone. An economy is not an end in itself. It is a system for helping human beings flourish on a living planet, and a system should be judged by whether it actually does its job. An economy that produces record corporate profits alongside record rates of financial anxiety among working families, that has more billionaires (and now trillionaires) than at any point in human history while half of Americans cannot cover a $1,000 emergency without debt -- that economy is failing at its core function, regardless of what the stock market says. I have spent years working in cooperative economics -- the Mondragon model, community land trusts, employee ownership structures -- and I know from direct experience that the argument that worker ownership is impractical is simply not true. It works. The economy we should be building creates owners, builders, workers, farmers, inventors, and entrepreneurs, not simply a class of financial intermediaries extracting rent from every transaction between producers and consumers. That requires enforcing antitrust laws with seriousness, supporting cooperatives and ESOPs, investing in apprenticeships in every trade that needs workers, raising the minimum wage to reflect what dignity actually costs, and strengthening the labor movement -- one of the few historical forces that has consistently and effectively counterbalanced concentrated economic power. 07 | A Thriving Planet Is National Security. Healthy soil, clean water, a stable climate, and resilient food systems are not luxuries or ideological preferences. They are the physical substrate on which every other human project depends. When I practice permaculture, I am not doing something radical -- I am doing something ancient: taking responsibility for the ground I stand on, so that it can sustain what comes after me. That same ethic, applied at national scale, looks like treating climate resilience as critical infrastructure rather than as a political controversy. It looks like transitioning to clean energy not because it is fashionable but because energy independence and supply-chain resilience are strategic imperatives. It looks like supporting regenerative agriculture and local food systems, protecting public lands from privatization, fully funding FEMA and disaster preparedness, and leading -- rather than abandoning -- international climate cooperation. The communities hit hardest by drought, flood, and wildfire are overwhelmingly the communities least able to recover on their own. Climate justice is not a slogan. It is the accurate description of who pays the price when we get this wrong. 08 | Government That Actually Works. Government exists because there are things free people cannot accomplish alone: issuing currency, defending the country, maintaining the rule of law, building infrastructure, responding to disasters, providing a social safety net, and preventing any private entity from becoming so powerful it can override the public interest. Those are real and legitimate functions. They require a government that is competent, transparent, and genuinely oriented toward solving problems -- rather than protecting insiders, serving donors, or perpetuating its own dysfunction. The opposite of corrupt government is not "no government." It is GOOD government: agencies that operate honestly and transparently, oversight that genuinely protects the public interest, public services that deliver what they promise, and Representatives who are accountable to constituents rather than to the industries they're supposed to regulate. We need to end the revolving door between government and the private sector. End gerrymandering. Enact ranked-choice voting, so people can vote for who they really want without fear of "spoilers". Measure what government actually delivers for people, and hold it accountable when it doesn't. These are achievable reforms. They require political will -- and Representatives willing to apply that will in service to the American people, even against their own institutional interests when necessary. Why Repair, and Not Revolution I want to be precise about why I use the word repair rather than transform or reimagine or any of the other words that get attached to political ambition. It is thoughtfulness. It is honesty. It is a statement of relationship. You repair something because you believe it is worth saving. Because its original design contains something valuable, even if it was imperfect to start with, even if years of neglect or intentional abuse have compromised its function. The American Constitution, despite its shortcomings, is a serious and sophisticated attempt to build a government that cannot be permanently captured by any faction, that cannot be inherited by dynasties, that must continuously re-earn the consent of the governed. The American ideals of liberty, equality, and justice under law -- imperfectly realized from the beginning, yes, and requiring ongoing work to extend to everyone they were supposed to include -- are worth fighting for. Not as they exist now, but as they were meant to be. As they should be. America is not disposable. She is not broken beyond repair. But she will not repair herself. And the people who profit from her remaining broken -- who benefit from a campaign finance system that makes corruption legal, from monopolies that face no competition, from wars that generate private profit for weapons companies and corrupt politicians, from a healthcare system that bankrupts you for being sick or injured -- have every incentive to convince you that either nothing is wrong or nothing can be done. Both of those claims are false. Policy made the system that is failing you. Policy, written by Representatives who are genuinely accountable to you rather than to corporate donors, can repair it. That is not a utopian promise. It is natural reality. It's an observation about how democratic self-governance is supposed to work. It is past time we made it work that way again. Melissa Chaudhry is a proven "Lioness for Justice," pro-se litigant and winner, Constitutional Democrat, community-rooted leader, published author, and public servant running for Washington's 9th Congressional District. The daughter of a retired US Naval Commander and international humanitarian physician, and the wife of a Melissa 's family story spans the full sweep of American history: her mother's roots trace to the Mayflower; her grandfather survived more than two years of Nazi concentration camp torture before coming to the US without papers. He died of those wounds in America. She 's invested twenty years of her life learning what it actually takes to design economic, political, and societal systems that provide dignity, safety, and opportunity for all people on a living planet. She worked professionally in affordable housing, climate resilience, sustainable agriculture, ecological design, public health, addiction treatment, poverty alleviation, and immigrant support. She spent years researching and writing weekly Global Geopolitical Human Security reports distributed to thousands of senior US officials and ambassadors worldwide. She has taught farming, resilient food systems, aquaponics, green infrastructure, and cooperative economics across multiple continents -- and in her own community, she repairs homes, gardens, and vehicles free of charge for friends, elderly and poor. When her honorable, 100% disabled American Military veteran husband, Zahid Chaudhry -- the disabled veteran in wheelchair who has been in America for 30+ years, always come here legally, never broken any US laws EVER, and has had his citizenship -- was illegally abducted and detained by ICE in 2025, she singlehandedly fought Pro Se across four federal courts and jurisdictions, up against the weaponized federal government, Justice Department, US Attorney General, and ICEsimultaneously , for four months until a federal judge called his detention "flat out wrong." She and her husband live in South Seattle with their two small children. She is the author of . Learn more about her campaign - and sign up to volunteer! - at.
